Orientation only; not used for any row.
Wikipedia, 'Kenenisa Bekele' (orientation only; not used as support for any row).

World Athletics Spikes, 'The Underdog' by Cathal Dennehy (20 April 2018, read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: three Olympic golds and world titles on track and cross country, the 5000 m and 10,000 m world records, and his move to the marathon with his results from Paris 2014 to London 2017, including the two non-finishes; includes his own stated aim of a marathon world record, which is self-statement.

IAAF (World Athletics) news report by David Powell, Beijing, 24 August 2008 (read in full): his Olympic-record wins in the 10,000 m (27:01.17) and 5000 m (12:57.82) at Beijing, the first Ethiopian to do that double since Miruts Yifter in 1980, his second Olympic 10,000 m title after Athens 2004, and his world records at both distances.

NAMPA/ANA wire report 'More to come from Bekele', as published by Republikein (18 November 2019, read in full): his stop-start marathon record (2014 Paris debut win, 2016 Berlin win, sixth in London 2018), the two-month Nijmegen preparation with physiotherapy, nutrition and monitored training arranged by his manager, weekly mileage rising from about 45 km to 150 km, and the 2:01:41 Berlin win in September 2019, two seconds off the world record; includes quotes from his manager and from him.

Marathon Handbook, 'How Kenenisa Bekele Used 5k And 10k Training To Set New Masters Marathon Record' by Jessy Carveth (read in full): the session types he shared for his 2019 Berlin build-up (short intervals such as 12 x 300 m and 30 x 400 m alongside marathon work), and his fourth place in 2:04:19 at Valencia 2023, reported as a masters world record, where he said he believed he could still improve.
Wikimedia Commons file page 'File:2024 London Marathon - Kenenisa Bekele.jpg' (checked for the portrait only; not used for any scoring).

adaptability.rationale: [src_bekele_spikes, src_bekele_nampa, src_bekele_handbook, src_bekele_iaaf2008 | 2008-2023 | governing-body feature + wire report + running press] After his 2008 track double (IAAF) he said it was too early to think of the marathon; by 2014 he had moved up and won his Paris debut (Spikes, NAMPA). For Berlin 2019 his team rebuilt his preparation around a two-month Nijmegen camp with nutrition and physiotherapy support and a rise from about 45 km to 150 km a week (NAMPA), and he mixed 5000 m and 10,000 m-style intervals into marathon training (Marathon Handbook). Change of event and method is documented by three independent outlets; the reasons given are partly his manager's and his own.

persistence.rationale: [src_bekele_spikes, src_bekele_nampa | 2016-2019 | governing-body feature + wire report] Spikes lists two non-finishes in his last three marathons at April 2018 and NAMPA records a sixth place in London 2018, yet NAMPA reports he returned with a new preparation and won Berlin in September 2019 in 2:01:41, two seconds off the world record; Spikes quotes his continued stated aim of the marathon record. Results and the comeback are reported independently; no health detail is used.

discipline.rationale: [src_bekele_nampa, src_bekele_handbook, src_bekele_spikes | 2018-2023 | wire report + running press + governing-body feature] NAMPA reports weekly mileage of about 150 km in the monitored Nijmegen build-up with daily feedback on meals to his team; Marathon Handbook lists the structured sessions he shared (for example 12 x 300 m, 30 x 400 m, 20 accelerations in the taper); Spikes also gives build-up weeks above 150 km. Training load and structure are documented, but the sources are largely the team's and his own account, so this is an inference about discipline.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_bekele_iaaf2008, src_bekele_spikes, src_bekele_handbook | 2004-2023 | governing-body report + feature + running press] IAAF documents Olympic-record wins in the 5000 m and 10,000 m at Beijing and a second Olympic 10,000 m title; Spikes quotes him saying the marathon world record is his main motivation, and Marathon Handbook has him at 41 running a reported masters record and saying he can still do better. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.53 because the motivation claims are his own statements and the results show performance rather than drive itself.
